title: Does Your Team Need a Charter?
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership field note argues that team charters, revived by the strains of dispersed and hybrid work, are valuable because they convert implicit assumptions about how a team works into explicit agreements. It locates most team dysfunction not in a lack of talent but in members holding different ideas about how to work together and resolve differences, and lists warning signs such as unnecessary conflict, ambiguous roles, slow decisions and low candor. The piece names the core ingredients of a charter, including purpose, boundaries, roles, decision rights, norms and measures of success, and translates them into a set of questions teams answer together. It insists that a charter must be built through team dialogue rather than handed down, that members should publicly commit to it, and that it should be revisited as a living document. It closes with a measured claim: a charter will not make a team great on its own, but it makes hard conversations easier and commitments harder to forget.
points: The note locates most team problems in differing, unspoken assumptions about how to work together rather than in skill gaps.
Its diagnostic questions include who owns which decisions and who has final authority when the team disagrees.
A charter imposed by the leader is ruled out; it has to be built through team dialogue, sometimes across several meetings.
Public commitment is presented as what keeps a charter from becoming a document people nod at and then ignore.
quotes: A team charter can be highly valuable because it turns implicit assumptions into explicit agreements.
Many team problems aren’t caused by a lack of talent or skills. They arise from people having different ideas about how the team should work together and resolve differences.
A charter should never be handed down by a leader but created through team dialogue. This sometimes takes several meetings or conversations.

Once the charter exists and is documented, team members must publicly commit to it. Otherwise, the charter becomes a document people nod at in the meeting and quietly ignore once the real work begins.
But even done well, a charter won’t make your team great on its own. What it does do is make hard conversations easier, decisions faster, and commitments harder to forget.
Most teams leave the way they work together unspoken and to chance. A charter is simply the decision not to.
